Brightness adjustment (decrease): Compute mean pixel brightness of both images (e.g., convert to grayscale and average pixel values) and assert the edited image has a lower mean brightness than the reference.

To isolate brightness change from structural edits, normalize both images to the same target brightness before comparing structure; use MSE or SSIM on the normalized versions to confirm the image content is otherwise unchanged.
Use PIL/Pillow ImageStat or manual numpy mean on the grayscale array as a reliable brightness proxy; avoid relying on histogram peaks which can be misleading for natural photos.
Compare mean pixel brightness of output image vs. input using PIL ImageStat; output mean should be lower than input mean.
Saturation/color vibrancy adjustment (in: Convert images to HSV mode using PIL's Image.convert('HSV') and compare mean S-channel values to verify saturation increased
Use SSIM on the H (hue) and V (value) channels to confirm image structure is preserved while only saturation changed
The measure_saturation helper computes mean pixel value of the S channel from an HSV image; structure_check_by_ssim wraps skimage.metrics.structural_similarity for channel-wise comparison
Convert output image to HSV/HSL with PIL or colorsys; compare mean saturation channel value against input — higher saturation indicates successful adjustment.
Export/save image to a specific file pat: Use os.path.isfile to confirm the exported file exists at the target path before any image comparison.
Compare exported image content against a reference using SSIM (structure_check_by_ssim) rather than exact pixel equality, since JPEG re-encoding introduces minor artifacts.
Both source and result images should be opened with PIL and passed to an SSIM-based structural similarity check; a threshold-based pass/fail is more robust than pixel-diff for lossy formats.
Use vm_file getter to retrieve the file from the expected path; verify it is a valid image with correct format using PIL.
Layer/object selection and repositioning: To verify an object is centered, load the exported image as a numpy array, isolate the object pixels by color (second most frequent color after background), compute the centroid of those pixels, compare centroid to image_center (shape[:2]/2), and check both axes are within a tolerance fraction (e.g., 5%) of image dimensions.
When identifying the object color programmatically, sort unique colors by pixel count ascending; the least-frequent non-background color is typically the foreground object.
np.argwhere on a boolean mask gives (row, col) coordinates; mean(axis=0) yields the centroid in (y, x) order matching image shape[:2].
Use PIL to inspect pixel positions in exported flat image; locate bounding box of target content (e.g., dark pixels for text) and verify its position relative to image width/height fractions
When verifying layer position, export/flatten the image and scan pixel rows/columns for content boundaries rather than relying on GIMP's internal layer offset metadata
Use gimp-drawable-offsets via Script-Fu or check flattened export to verify layer position; for centering, offsets should equal (canvas_w - layer_w)/2 and (canvas_h - layer_h)/2.
Hide/show docks (UI panel visibility): Read GIMP's sessionrc config file (~/.config/GIMP/2.10/sessionrc on Linux) and parse key-value pairs (lines wrapped in parentheses) to check boolean flags like 'hide-docks yes/no'; use the same line-splitting logic: strip parens, split on whitespace, compare items[0] to key and items[-1] to value.
Accessibility tree or screenshot comparison can detect dock panel presence; dockable-dialog visibility is hard to assert programmatically without screenshot diffing.
Background removal / transparency (alpha: Use SSIM-based structural similarity (check_structure_sim pattern) to compare the result PNG against a gold reference; images must match in size first, then structural content.
Verify the output is a PNG with an alpha channel (mode 'RGBA') and that background pixels have alpha=0, distinguishing true transparency from a white fill.
SSIM comparison on RGBA images should be done on the RGB channels or after compositing onto a neutral background to avoid alpha-channel noise skewing the score.
Image dimensions must be identical between result and reference before any similarity metric is meaningful; a size mismatch should immediately return 0.

Use SSIM (skimage.metrics.structural_similarity) with channel_axis=2 on RGB-converted arrays to compare background-removed outputs against a gold reference; resize source to target dimensions before comparison if sizes differ

When evaluating alpha-channel / background-removal results, convert both images to RGB before SSIM to avoid mode mismatch errors; the evaluator tolerates minor pixel differences with a threshold around 0.85

For pixel-art character extraction, the gold reference PNG will have transparent background; comparing SSIM after RGB conversion effectively checks structural fidelity of the extracted character region
Open exported PNG with PIL, convert to RGBA, check alpha channel values at expected transparent regions (e.g., corners or background pixels should have alpha==0).
Add new layer with custom name: GIMP stores the last-used new-layer name in gimprc as the key `layer-new-name`; parse gimprc lines (skip `#` comments and blank lines), strip surrounding parentheses, split on whitespace, and compare key token and value token (quoted string) to verify the layer name was set.

Use the `check_config_status` / `gimp_config_file` getter+checker pattern: retrieve `~/.config/GIMP/2.10/gimprc` from the VM, scan for the relevant key-value pair; a match returns 1.0, no match returns 0.0.
The gimprc value for layer names is stored as a quoted string (e.g., `"Square"`), so comparisons must include the surrounding double-quotes.
Use gimp-image-get-active-drawable or gimp-image-get-layers via Script-Fu to retrieve layer names and properties; compare against expected name strings.
Open filter dialog via menu (Filters > V: GIMP logs recently used actions in ~/.config/GIMP/2.10/action-history; check that file for the action identifier (e.g., 'filters-vignette') to confirm a filter dialog was opened, without needing screenshot comparison.
Verify vignette effect by sampling pixel brightness near image corners vs. center; corners should be darker after vignette application.
Preferences configuration (undo steps/le: GIMP preferences are persisted in gimprc (Linux: ~/.config/GIMP/2.10/gimprc); parse it by stripping parentheses and splitting tokens — each setting is a line like `(key value)`
Use check_config_status-style parsing: skip comment lines starting with '#', strip leading '(' and trailing ')', split on whitespace, then match items[0] as key and items[-1] as value
The undo-levels key stores the minimum undo steps; verify its integer value as a string token in gimprc after GIMP quits (config is written on exit)
Read GIMP's gimprc or preferences XML file from the VM using vm_file getter; parse the relevant config key (e.g., undo-levels) and compare its value.
Layer scaling/resizing with aspect ratio: Export the result and use PIL to open it; when the layer has transparency, use alpha.getbbox() to find the bounding box of non-transparent pixels and measure content height/width from that bbox rather than the full canvas size.

For structural correctness after resize, crop the reference image to its non-transparent content area, resize it to match the output dimensions, then compare with SSIM (structure_check_by_ssim pattern) to confirm the subject is visually intact.
check_image_size with ignore_transparent=True is the right metric family for layer-resize tasks where the layer sits on a transparent canvas—canvas size may differ from content size.
Aspect ratio preservation can be inferred indirectly: if the target height is met and SSIM against the original (rescaled) passes, the ratio was maintained without needing to assert the exact width.
Retrieve layer dimensions via Script-Fu gimp-drawable-width/height or check exported image size with PIL; verify width/height ratio matches original.
Image mode conversion to Palette/Indexed: Check PIL image mode == 'P' to confirm palette-based conversion; use structure_check_by_ssim after converting the palette image to RGB for structural similarity against a reference.
Open exported file with PIL and check img.mode == 'P'; verify palette length matches expected number of colors.
Text layer repositioning (move to specif: Export the canvas as a flat PNG, convert to grayscale, then scan pixel rows for dark-pixel x-coordinates to determine the leftmost/rightmost extent of text content
Define positional thresholds as fractions of total image width (e.g., left 5%) rather than absolute pixel values to stay resolution-agnostic
PIL pixel-scanning loops over (x, y) with an early break per row are sufficient to find the bounding edge of text content in a flat export
Use gimp-text-layer-get-text and gimp-drawable-offsets via Script-Fu, or flatten and inspect pixel regions for text presence using PIL.
Contrast adjustment (increase): Use a `calculate_contrast` helper (e.g., standard deviation of grayscale pixel values) to compare contrast between the modified and original image; the modified image must have a strictly higher value.

Use SSIM (skimage.metrics.structural_similarity) with a moderate threshold (~0.65) to confirm the image structure is preserved after contrast enhancement — resize both images to the same dimensions before comparison.
Contrast can be boosted via Colors > Brightness-Contrast, Colors > Curves, or Colors > Levels; all produce measurable increases in pixel value standard deviation.
Compare pixel value standard deviation of output vs. input using PIL ImageStat; higher std deviation indicates increased contrast.
Horizontal flip/mirror image: Use PIL's Image.transpose(Image.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT) on the original image and compare with the result using SSIM (threshold ~0.99) to confirm a horizontal mirror was applied
structure_check_by_ssim comparing the flipped source against the exported result handles minor JPEG/PNG re-encoding artifacts; use a high SSIM threshold (≥0.99) rather than pixel-exact equality
Export the result via GIMP's overwrite/export-as flow and load both source and result with PIL for comparison — format differences (JPEG→PNG) are tolerable as long as structural similarity is high
Compare left-column pixels of output with right-column pixels of input (and vice versa) using PIL to confirm horizontal mirroring.
Theme configuration (dark/light theme sw: Read the gimprc config file (~/.config/GIMP/2.10/gimprc on Linux) and parse lines as space-separated tokens stripped of parentheses; look for a key-value pair where the key token matches 'theme' and the value token matches the expected theme string (e.g., '"Light"' or '"Dark"')

The check_config_status pattern is reusable for any gimprc preference: skip comment lines starting with '#', strip surrounding parentheses, split on whitespace, then compare items[0] to key and items[-1] to value — works for single-key and two-token-key rules alike
Read GIMP's gimprc or theme config file from the VM; check the theme key value matches expected theme name string.
Fill layer with solid color (bucket fill: Load the exported PNG with PIL/numpy and iterate over pixels; identify background pixels using a reference image (e.g., non-object pixels are non-black in the reference), then verify each corresponding pixel in the result satisfies the target color condition (e.g., green channel dominates both red and blue channels).
When the task involves selective layer filling, compare pixel-by-pixel against a reference image to distinguish object pixels from background pixels before asserting color values.
Use numpy array indexing on RGBA or RGB pixel arrays; check channel relationships (g > r and g > b for green) rather than exact RGB tuples to handle shade variations of the target color.
Sample pixel color at multiple points in the filled region using PIL; all sampled pixels should match the expected fill color within tolerance.
Animated GIF export from video frames: Use PIL/Pillow to open the output GIF and check that it has multiple frames (n_frames > 1), confirming animation was created rather than a static image.
Compare the first frame of the output GIF against the reference GIF using grayscale SSIM (as done here); resize both to the smaller dimension before comparison to handle minor resolution differences.
For multi-frame GIFs, comparing only the first frame via SSIM is a practical proxy for content correctness when full frame-by-frame comparison is too strict.
When verifying GIF content derived from a video clip, SSIM scores in the 0.7–0.9 range typically indicate correct source segment; scores below 0.5 suggest wrong time offset or wrong source video.
PIL's Image.seek(n) can iterate frames; checking frame count and representative frame similarity covers both structure and content without exact pixel matching.
Check exported GIF with PIL: verify n_frames > 1 and frame dimensions match expected canvas size.
Copy image to clipboard for use in other: When verifying that a GIMP image was copied and pasted into a docx, use python-docx to extract embedded image blobs via doc.part.rels and compare pixel data with Image.tobytes(); count equality and pixel-level equality are both needed.
Images embedded in docx are stored as relationship parts; iterate doc.part.rels.values() filtering by 'image' in rel.reltype to extract all images regardless of paragraph/inline placement.
Pixel-exact comparison (tobytes()) is stricter than size comparison; if the copy-paste pipeline introduces re-encoding, consider tolerance-based comparison or format normalization before comparing.
Use xclip or xsel command-line tools via vm_command_line getter to inspect clipboard content type/format.
Brightness adjustment (increase): Use PIL to compute mean brightness of the output image (convert to grayscale, call stat().mean or np.array mean) and compare against the original; the output must have a higher mean brightness value.

After brightness-normalizing both images to the same target brightness, compute MSE between them to confirm structural similarity is preserved despite the brightness change — use a small MSE threshold (e.g. 0.03–0.15 depending on image size).

The check_brightness_decrease_and_structure_sim pattern (despite its name) is reused for increase tasks by swapping src/tgt order: verify brightness_tgt > brightness_src where tgt is the user-produced file and src is the reference original.
Compare mean pixel brightness of output image vs. input using PIL ImageStat; output mean should be higher than input mean.
Export/save image as PDF: Use PyMuPDF (fitz) to extract embedded images from both the result and reference PDFs, then compare them using perceptual hashing (e.g., imagehash.phash) with a small hash-difference threshold to allow minor encoding variations
Check that the PDF contains the same number of embedded images as the reference; a mismatch in image count should score 0
When the PDF contains no embedded images (e.g., vector-only or text-only), treat it as a special case separate from image-based comparison
Check file existence and use a PDF parser (e.g., PyPDF2 or pdfplumber) to verify page count and approximate page dimensions.
Multi-step image editing from written in: Use SSIM-based grayscale comparison against a reference image; resize both to the smaller dimension before computing similarity to handle minor resolution differences.

When the task involves reading instructions from a document (e.g., LibreOffice Writer) and applying them in GIMP, the evaluator should compare the output image structurally/visually rather than checking individual edit parameters, since the exact combination of edits is unknown without parsing the instruction document.

The compare_images metric converts both images to grayscale and resizes to the smaller size before SSIM comparison, so color-only changes may score high even if incorrect; be aware this metric is relatively permissive for color edits.
need_rule_judge=true signals a human or LLM rule judge is also applied alongside the automated SSIM score, useful when the edit combination is complex or ambiguous.
Break verification into per-step checks: image size, layer count, pixel color samples, and metadata; use PIL for pixel-level and file-level assertions.
Script-Fu image resize and export: Use check_image_size metric with PIL Image.open on the exported file; verify img.size matches (width, height) exactly. For Script-Fu execution results, the output file existence and correct dimensions are the primary signals.
JPEG export with compression/quality red: Use os.path.getsize() to verify the output file is strictly below the required byte threshold; no image library needed for the size check itself.
When resizing is also permitted, verify the file is a valid JPEG (e.g., PIL Image.open + verify) in addition to the size check, to confirm it wasn't just truncated.
GIMP Script-Fu export quality parameter (0–100) directly controls JPEG file size; evaluators can test multiple quality levels programmatically if needed.
Image slicing and section rearrangement: Use SSIM-based structural similarity (check_structure_sim pattern) to compare output PNG against a gold reference; both images must have identical pixel dimensions before SSIM is computed, so verify size equality first.

When verifying column-reorder tasks, compare horizontal strip statistics (mean color per column band) between output and reference to confirm warm-tone gradient ordering without relying on exact pixel values.
Script-Fu or command-line gimp batch (gimp -i -b) can crop, reorder, and flatten sections; verify the exported file exists at the expected path and is a valid PNG before structural comparison.
Crop image (remove percentage from edge): Use SSIM-based structural similarity after verifying exact pixel dimensions match; both size equality and structural content must pass for a crop operation to be considered correct.
When cropping a percentage from an edge, verify the output height equals (1 - crop_fraction) * original_height and width is unchanged before running SSIM comparison.
check_structure_sim returns 1.0 only when sizes match AND structure_check_by_ssim passes, so evaluators must ensure the crop produces the exact expected dimensions, not just visually similar content.
Extract transaction data from image file: Use PIL/Pillow or similar to open image files and verify readable content; for evaluator purposes, the key check is whether numeric values extracted from images match expected amounts within a tolerance (approx matching).

When transactions are sourced from images, verify that OCR or manual extraction produces values matching expected numeric amounts; use approx-tolerance checks (e.g., within 0.1) rather than exact equality for currency values.
Identify and filter images by subject/pe: Use compare_image_list (pixel-diff via ImageChops.difference + getbbox) to verify correct images were selected; mismatched sizes are handled by resizing pred to gold before comparison.
When the task produces a zip, postconfig typically unzips it first so individual image files can be fetched via get_vm_file for comparison against gold references.
For multi-image checks, all images in the list must match exactly (all-or-nothing score of 1.0 or 0.0), so verify the complete set of selected images, not just a subset.

Use image content hashing (e.g., SHA256) to map each file to its identity, then check the resulting filename against a list of acceptable name variants (case-insensitive, with/without extension, with/without spaces).
Identify landmarks/locations depicted in: Verification uses a script that hashes image file contents and maps hashes to expected filename variants; check that each image file's new name (with or without extension, any case) appears in the accepted-names list for its hash.
The accepted-names list should include common alternate names, local names, and partial names for the landmark, since AI identification may return any recognized variant.
Use expect_in_result mode with per-hash lists of acceptable filenames so that any reasonable identification is accepted rather than requiring an exact single answer.
